Name: Ear
Attributes: {"note": "Pretty stable, semantically and also against erosion. Little probability to get borrowed from another language!"}

Name: Nose
Attributes: {"note": "Very stable word, with little exposure to semantic shift and moderate daily use. Probably the best suited word for comparative linguistics!"}

Name: Hand
Attributes: {"note": "As many other parts of the body, little exposure to borrowing and good semantic stability. However, in many languages, the meaning shift from \"hand\" to \"arm\" or the other way round."}

Name: Tongue
Attributes: {"note": "Very stable - similar to nose, although it is also being used for \"language\" in many languages and gives it an exposure to semantic shift or at least to confusion."}

Name: Tooth
Attributes: {"note": "Very stable - similar conditions as \"nose\". However, this word has been subject to semantic shift in parts of the Indo-European family - with a mix \"Tooth\"/\"Tongue\" (\"-Z-B-\" in Slavic/Indo-Iranan languages)."}

Name: Death
Attributes: {"note": "As an abstract concept, the use of this word for comparing remote languages is somewhat hazardous. However, it is the one best linking the Indo-Europea and Semitic language families (Arabic \u0627\u0644\u0645\u0648\u062a (mut)/ Hebrew \u05de\u05d5\u05d5\u05ea (mavet) -> French \"Mort\" / Slavic \"Mertv\"... In some languages, the root of the verb \"to die\" has been taken instead of the substantive \"death\" when it was not available (\"to die\" is an element of the Swadesh list \"death\" is not)"}

Name: Water
Attributes: {"note": "Very interesting word, although it is in intensive use and as such subject to more erosion. Moreover, semantic shift exposure is higher than for body parts. Water is the word best linking the Indo-European and Finno-Ugric language families (Finnish \"Vesi\" / Hungarian \"Vez\" -> German \"Wasser\" / Slavic \"Voda\")"}

Name: Sun
Attributes: {"note": "This word has a big exposure to semantic shift but delivers good results in comparative linguistics. Probably less suited for remote language relationships"}

Name: Wind
Attributes: {"note": "As all nature related words, should have existed in early languages."}

Name: Two

Name: Three

Name: Four
Attributes: {"note": "Little exposure to semantic shift but intensive use in daily life (\"erosion\"). Exposure to borrowing similar to \"three\"."}

Name: I
Attributes: {"note": "Very high exposure to erosion (intensive use in daily life) but little chance of semantic shift. Another problem with \"I\" is that it is monosyllabic in many languages - and monosyllabic resemblances between two languages are statistically more exposed to chance resemblance."}
